title: Name the Room Not the Movie
bigQuestion: How can we tell what a real school, person or style was, when films have told the story louder?

story.title: A Poster and a Charter
story.kicker: A film poster and a club's founding papers use the same name in different ways.
paragraphs: A library display holds two items side by side. The first is a poster for Fist of Fury, a Hong Kong film from 1972. It stars Bruce Lee. The poster shows the name of a real Shanghai club, Jingwu, in large letters.

The second item is a copy of papers about that same club. They record that the Jingwu Athletic Association was founded in Shanghai in 1910. They list members, officers and the styles taught. They describe a public club for exercise and training.

The film tells a story set around the club after Huo Yuanjia's death. Its hero, Chen Zhen, is a character written for the screen. The papers describe the club's real founding and the people who ran it.

Both items use the word Jingwu. One is a story made to move an audience. The other is a record made to run an institution. A historian reads each one for what it can honestly show, and checks names and dates against the club's own papers.
story.think: If you only saw the poster, what might you believe about Jingwu that the papers would change?

lessons.title: Wong Fei-hung the Doctor
lessons.mainIdea: Wong Fei-hung was a real doctor and teacher in Guangdong, and films turned him into a legend.
reading: Wong Fei-hung lived from 1847 to 1924 in Guangdong Province, in southern China. He learned the Hung Gar style from his father, Wong Kei-ying. He practiced traditional Chinese medicine and ran a clinic called Po Chi Lam in Foshan.

Starting in 1949, Hong Kong studios made a long series of films about him. The actor Kwan Tak-hing played him in dozens of them. In 1991 director Tsui Hark made Once Upon a Time in China, with Jet Li as Wong. Each film invented new adventures.

A *biography* is a true account of a person's life, based on records. A *folk hero* is a real or imagined person whose story grows as people retell it. Wong Fei-hung is both. Historians separate the doctor in Foshan from the hero on the screen.

words.d: a true account of a person's life, built from records
a person whose story grows larger as people retell it in songs, books or films

look.title: Two Descriptions of One Man
look.text: Description A: a doctor born in 1847 who ran a clinic in Foshan and taught his father's style. Description B: a hero who defeats a new villain in each film, from the 1949 series to the 1990s.
look.prompt: Which description could a historian check in records? What would you look for?

check.q: What was Wong Fei-hung's work in real life?
choices: a doctor of traditional Chinese medicine and a teacher
check.why: Wong Fei-hung ran the Po Chi Lam clinic in Foshan and taught Hung Gar.

check.q: Which actor played Wong in dozens of films from 1949?
check.why: Kwan Tak-hing played Wong Fei-hung in a long series starting in 1949.

check.q: What is a folk hero?
choices: a person whose story grows as people retell it
a judge in a taolu event
check.why: A folk hero is a real or imagined person whose story grows larger with retelling.

lessons.title: Huo Yuanjia and a Screen Student
lessons.mainIdea: Huo Yuanjia was a real martial artist linked to Jingwu; his famous film student Chen Zhen was invented.
reading: Huo Yuanjia was a martial artist from Tianjin, in northern China. He is linked to the founding of the Jingwu Athletic Association in Shanghai. He died in 1910. Stories about him say he took on foreign strongmen who issued public challenges.

In 1972 Fist of Fury, made by Golden Harvest in Hong Kong, told a story set after his death. Bruce Lee played Chen Zhen, a student who seeks justice. Chen Zhen is a *fictional* character, created for the film. The film shows Japanese characters mocking the Chinese as weak.

The film spoke to anger about foreign power in China in the early 1900s. It was made for audiences in Hong Kong, then a British colony, and across Asia. In 2006 Jet Li starred in Fearless, another film about Huo. It too mixed record and invention.

words.d: made up for a story; not a real person or event
a place ruled by a distant country; Hong Kong was a British colony until 1997

look.title: Record or Screen?
look.text: Sort these facts. 1. Huo Yuanjia died in 1910. 2. Chen Zhen returns to avenge his teacher. 3. Jingwu was founded in Shanghai. 4. Fist of Fury was made in Hong Kong in 1972.
look.prompt: Which of the four facts is about a fictional person? Which are about real records?

check.q: Who was Chen Zhen?
choices: the founder of the Guoshu Institute
a fictional student created for Fist of Fury
check.why: Chen Zhen is a fictional character written for the 1972 film Fist of Fury.

check.q: When did Huo Yuanjia die?
check.why: Huo Yuanjia died in 1910, the year Jingwu was founded.

check.q: What was Hong Kong's status when Fist of Fury was made?
check.why: Hong Kong was a British colony until 1997.

lessons.title: Ip Man in Hong Kong
lessons.mainIdea: Ip Man taught Wing Chun in Hong Kong from the 1950s; films about him came decades after his death.
reading: Ip Man was born in Foshan, Guangdong, in 1893. He learned Wing Chun there. After 1949 he moved to Hong Kong, where he began teaching Wing Chun in the early 1950s. He died in Hong Kong in 1972.

In Hong Kong, Ip Man taught in rented rooms and rooftops, and his students opened schools of their own. One of his students was a teenager named Bruce Lee. Through students who moved abroad, Ip Man's *lineage* reached Europe, North America and Australia.

In 2008 the film Ip Man, starring Donnie Yen, made him famous to millions who had never heard of him. It added invented fights and events. Sequels followed. Many new students came to Wing Chun schools because of the films, and teachers had to explain what was history and what was screen story.

words.d: a southern Chinese martial art from Guangdong, taught in Hong Kong by Ip Man and his students
a line of teachers and students that passes an art from one generation to the next

look.title: Ip Man: Life and Screen
rows: Ip Man dies in Hong Kong
look.cite: Hong Kong Film Archive; Ip Man biographies
look.prompt: How many years after his death did the first Ip Man film appear?

check.q: Where did Ip Man teach Wing Chun from the 1950s?
check.why: Ip Man moved to Hong Kong after 1949 and taught Wing Chun there.

check.q: What is a lineage?
choices: a line of teachers and students
check.why: A lineage is the line of teachers and students that passes an art down.

check.q: What did the 2008 film Ip Man add to his story?
check.why: The film made Ip Man famous but added invented fights and events.

lessons.title: Bruce Lee Between School and Screen
lessons.mainIdea: Bruce Lee ran real schools in the United States and named his own approach Jeet Kune Do in 1967.
reading: Bruce Lee was born in San Francisco in 1940 and grew up in Hong Kong. He studied Wing Chun with Ip Man. In 1959 he moved to the United States. In Seattle he opened a school and called his teaching Jun Fan Gung Fu. He later taught in Oakland and Los Angeles.

Lee taught students who were not Chinese, at a time when some teachers in Chinatowns taught only Chinese students. In 1967 he gave his own approach a name: *Jeet Kune Do*. The name means way of the intercepting fist in Cantonese. He called it a way of thinking about fighting rather than a fixed style.

His films The Big Boss (1971), Fist of Fury (1972) and Enter the Dragon (1973) made him a world star. He died in Hong Kong in July 1973, at age 32, just before Enter the Dragon opened. Enter the Dragon was made by Warner Bros. with Golden Harvest, a Hong Kong studio.

words.d: the name Bruce Lee gave his approach in 1967; Cantonese for way of the intercepting fist
a neighborhood in a city outside China where many Chinese families live and run businesses

look.title: Bruce Lee's Two Careers
look.cite: Bruce Lee Foundation; Matthew Polly, Bruce Lee: A Life (2018)
look.prompt: Did Lee name his approach before or after he became a film star?

check.q: Where was Bruce Lee born?
check.why: Bruce Lee was born in San Francisco in 1940 and grew up in Hong Kong.

check.q: What year did Lee name Jeet Kune Do?
check.why: Lee named his approach Jeet Kune Do in 1967, before his biggest films.

check.q: Who taught Bruce Lee Wing Chun?
check.why: Lee studied Wing Chun with Ip Man in Hong Kong.

lessons.title: Studios and Shaolin Films
lessons.mainIdea: Hong Kong studios made Shaolin a famous film setting, and a 1982 film sent crowds of visitors to the real temple.
reading: In the 1960s and 1970s, Hong Kong studios such as Shaw Brothers made many martial arts films. A *genre* is a type of film with familiar settings and stories. Shaolin became one of the genre's favorite settings. The 36th Chamber of Shaolin, from Shaw Brothers in 1978, showed a hero training through many halls.

Those halls were a film set. The real temple's records do not list thirty-six chambers. Films borrowed the temple's name and its legends, then invented new ones. Audiences in Hong Kong, Southeast Asia and later the West came to picture Shaolin through these sets.

In 1982 the film Shaolin Temple, starring a young Jet Li, was shot partly at the real monastery in Henan. It was a huge hit in China. Visitors poured into Dengfeng, and new martial arts schools opened near the temple. A film changed a real place.

words.d: a type of film or book with familiar settings and stories, such as westerns or martial arts films
a large Hong Kong film studio that made many martial arts films in the 1960s and 1970s

look.title: The Set and the Site
look.text: Picture a film set built in a Hong Kong studio: painted walls, many training halls, a gate with the word Shaolin. Now picture the real monastery on Mount Song: old halls, a forest of stone stupas for monks, and steles from the Tang dynasty.
look.prompt: What could a visitor learn at the real site that the film set cannot show?

check.q: What is a genre?
choices: a type of film with familiar settings and stories
check.why: A genre is a type of film, like the martial arts film, with familiar settings and stories.

check.q: What happened after the 1982 film Shaolin Temple?
choices: Visitors poured into Dengfeng and new schools opened
Wushu became an Olympic medal sport
The temple moved to Hong Kong
check.why: The hit film drew crowds of visitors and new schools to the area around the real temple.

check.q: Which studio made The 36th Chamber of Shaolin?
check.why: Shaw Brothers released The 36th Chamber of Shaolin in 1978.

lessons.title: Kung Fu on American Television
lessons.mainIdea: The ABC series Kung Fu (1972 to 1975) spread the English word widely and cast a white actor as its Chinese American hero.
reading: From 1972 to 1975, the ABC network aired a series called Kung Fu. Its hero was a Shaolin-trained monk of Chinese and white American parents. He wandered the American West in the 1800s. The show made the word kung fu familiar in millions of American homes.

The lead was played by David Carradine, a white actor. Many Asian American actors and viewers criticized the choice. They pointed out that Asian actors were rarely offered lead roles on American television. This practice of casting white actors in Asian roles is often called *whitewashing*.

The show was set in a real time: Chinese workers did help build the American West, including the Central Pacific Railroad in the 1860s. But its Shaolin scenes came from legend and the studio. It is evidence about 1970s television, not about Shaolin.

words.d: casting white actors to play characters of color, or leaving people of color out of a story
a television show that tells stories in many episodes over time

look.title: What a Show Is Evidence Of
look.text: A 1973 TV guide lists an episode of Kung Fu. It names the network, the star and the time slot. A letter to a newspaper from the same year complains that the star is not Asian.
look.prompt: What do these two documents tell a historian about the 1970s? What do they not tell about Shaolin?

check.q: Which network aired the series Kung Fu?
check.why: The ABC network aired Kung Fu from 1972 to 1975.

check.q: Why did many Asian American actors criticize the show?
choices: A white actor played its Chinese American hero
check.why: They criticized casting David Carradine, a white actor, when Asian actors rarely got lead roles.

check.q: What is the show best evidence of?
check.why: The show tells historians about 1970s TV; its Shaolin scenes came from legend and the studio.

lessons.title: One Style, Many Spellings
lessons.mainIdea: Different spellings of one style's name, like Wing Chun, Ving Tsun and Wing Tsun, often mark different organizations.
reading: Chinese is written in characters, not letters. When a name is written in Latin letters, people must choose a spelling system. *Romanization* is the name for writing a language in the Latin alphabet. Cantonese and Mandarin also sound different.

One style can have many spellings. After Ip Man's death, his students' groups in Hong Kong and abroad used Wing Chun, Ving Tsun and Wing Tsun. The Ving Tsun Athletic Association was founded in Hong Kong in 1967 by Ip Man and his students. Some groups registered their spelling as a *trademark*.

A spelling can work like a family name. It can tell you which organization a school belongs to. So when a school sign uses a certain spelling, a historian asks which association uses it, and who gave that school's teacher the right to teach.

words.d: writing a language, such as Chinese, in the Latin alphabet
a name or symbol a group registers by law so others may not use it for the same service

look.title: Three Signs on One Street
look.text: One street has three schools. The first sign reads Wing Chun Kung Fu. The second reads Ving Tsun Athletic Club. The third reads Wing Tsun Academy. All three say they come from Ip Man.
look.prompt: What questions would you ask each school to learn which organization it belongs to?

check.q: What is romanization?
choices: writing a language in the Latin alphabet
check.why: Romanization means writing a language like Chinese in Latin letters.

check.q: When was the Ving Tsun Athletic Association founded?
check.why: Ip Man and his students founded the Ving Tsun Athletic Association in Hong Kong in 1967.

check.q: What can a school's spelling tell you?
choices: the exact date of a film
which organization the school may belong to
the weight class of its students
which temple it was built in
check.why: Different spellings are often used by different associations, like a family name.

lessons.title: Ranks on Paper: Duan Wei
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1990s the Chinese Wushu Association created the duan wei system of written ranks for wushu.
reading: Older Chinese arts did not use colored belts. A student's place came from the teacher and the lineage. Belts and dan grades came from Japanese judo, where Kanō Jigorō began them in the 1880s.

In the late 1990s the Chinese Wushu Association launched the *duan wei* system. Duan means level and wei means rank. It has nine levels in three groups, marked on certificates. The goal was one national standard across many styles.

A *certificate* is a written record that an official body gives to a person. It names the holder, the rank and who awarded it. A historian can check a certificate against the body that issued it. A movie can give a hero a title, but it cannot issue a real rank.

words.d: the nine-level written rank system the Chinese Wushu Association created for wushu
a written record from an official body that names a person and what they earned

look.title: A Certificate to Read
look.text: A framed paper hangs in a school office. It names the teacher, a duan wei level, the date and the stamp of the Chinese Wushu Association. Next to it hangs a poster from a martial arts film with the words Grandmaster of the Temple.
look.prompt: Which item can be checked with an official body? How would you check it?

check.q: Who created the duan wei system?
check.why: The Chinese Wushu Association launched duan wei in the late 1990s.

check.q: How many levels does duan wei have?
check.why: Duan wei has nine levels, arranged in three groups.

check.q: Why can a historian check a certificate?
choices: It names the holder and the body that issued it
It is written by the student
check.why: A certificate names the holder, the rank and the issuing body, so it can be checked.

lessons.title: Films as Evidence of Their Time
lessons.mainIdea: Martial arts films are strong evidence about the years and places that made them, even when their stories are invented.
reading: A film is a *primary source* for the time it was made. Fist of Fury shows what Hong Kong filmmakers in 1972 wanted to say about foreign power in China. The Kung Fu series shows who American television cast in 1972.

Later films show later times. Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, directed by Ang Lee, won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film in 2001. It was made by companies in Taiwan, Hong Kong, mainland China and the United States. Its partners show how the film business had become global.

Kung Fu Panda, an American animated film from DreamWorks in 2008, set a cartoon story in an imagined China. Each film tells us about its makers and audiences. None of them is a record of how a real school was founded or who taught whom.

words.d: a document or object made at the time being studied
an American film prize, also called the Oscar, given each year since 1929

look.title: Films and Their Years
look.cite: Hong Kong Film Archive; Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences; studio release records
look.prompt: Pick one film. What was happening in its time and place that it might show?

check.q: What is a film a primary source for?
choices: the time and place it was made
check.why: A film is made at a certain time, so it is a primary source for that time and its makers.

check.q: Which film won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film in 2001?
check.why: Ang Lee's Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon won that award in 2001.

check.q: What can a film NOT prove on its own?
choices: what its makers wanted to say
check.why: A film tells about its makers and time, but a school's founding needs records such as charters and certificates.

lessons.title: Chinese Schools Abroad
lessons.mainIdea: Chinese emigrants carried martial arts to cities abroad, where schools and lion dance troupes served their communities.
reading: From the 1800s, many Chinese people left southern China for Southeast Asia, the Americas and Australia. Many came from Guangdong. A community living far from its homeland is called a *diaspora*.

In many Chinatowns, martial arts schools were tied to family and district associations. These schools often trained *lion dance* troupes, which perform at Lunar New Year, weddings and store openings. The lion dance carries meanings of good fortune in many Chinese communities.

After 1965, the United States changed its immigration law. The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 ended quotas based on national origin. More Chinese immigrants arrived, and more schools opened. Many of them taught southern styles and used Cantonese names.

words.d: a community living far from its homeland, and keeping ties to it
a Chinese performance with a costumed lion, often by martial arts school troupes at festivals

look.title: A 1965 Law
look.text: The act ended the system of quotas that set how many immigrants could come from each country based on national origin. It made family ties and job skills the main basis for entry.
look.cite: Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 (Hart-Celler Act), United States Congress
look.prompt: How might a change in immigration law change the martial arts schools in an American city?

check.q: What is a diaspora?
choices: a community living far from its homeland
check.why: A diaspora is a community far from its homeland that keeps ties to it.

check.q: When do lion dance troupes often perform?
choices: at Lunar New Year and openings
check.why: Lion dance troupes perform at Lunar New Year, weddings and store openings.

check.q: What did the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 end?
check.why: The 1965 act ended quotas based on national origin, and more Chinese immigrants arrived.

lessons.title: Questions for Any School Name
lessons.mainIdea: To check a school's name, historians ask for the place, the teacher line, the governing body and the documents.
reading: A school's name is a *claim*. It says where the art came from and who taught it. A historian checks a claim against records, the same way a detective checks a story against evidence.

Useful records include a charter or founding papers, certificates, photographs with dates, newspaper reports and letters. A charter is a document that creates an organization and states its purpose. Jingwu's founding in 1910 and the Ving Tsun Athletic Association's in 1967 are both on record.

Films, posters and legends are records too, but of something else. They show what people believed or enjoyed. When a film and a charter disagree about a school, the charter usually tells us more about the school, and the film tells us more about its audience.

words.d: a statement that something is true, which can be checked against evidence
a document that creates an organization and states its purpose

look.title: Four Questions
look.text: Question 1: Where did this art come from? Question 2: Who taught the teacher? Question 3: Which body, if any, gave the teacher a rank? Question 4: What papers or photos support the answers? A school sign says Shaolin Temple Kung Fu.
look.prompt: Which question would you ask first about this sign, and why?

check.q: What is a charter?
choices: a document that creates an organization
check.why: A charter creates an organization and states its purpose.

check.q: If a film and a charter disagree about a school, which usually tells more about the school?
check.why: The charter is a record made to run the school; the film tells more about its audience.

check.q: Which founding is on record, according to this lesson?
check.why: Jingwu's 1910 founding in Shanghai is on record; the others come from films or legends.

review.q: Which person in Fist of Fury was fictional?
review.why: Chen Zhen was created for the film; Huo Yuanjia was a real martial artist.

review.q: Where did Wong Fei-hung run his clinic?
review.why: Wong Fei-hung ran the Po Chi Lam clinic in Foshan, Guangdong.

review.q: What name did Bruce Lee give his approach in 1967?
review.why: Lee named his approach Jeet Kune Do in 1967.

choices: casting white actors in roles for people of color
review.why: Whitewashing means casting white actors to play characters of color.

review.q: What effect did the 1982 film Shaolin Temple have?
choices: It drew crowds and new schools to Dengfeng
review.why: The hit film brought many visitors and new schools to the area near the temple.

review.q: Why might three schools spell one style three ways?
choices: Spelling is random and means nothing
review.why: Wing Chun, Ving Tsun and Wing Tsun are used by different groups, much like family names.

review.q: Which is the best record of a school's founding?
review.why: A charter creates an organization and states its purpose, so it records the founding.

choices: a document or object made at the time studied
review.why: A primary source was made at the time being studied.
